lesson.intro: Before you configure anything, know what each box in a network diagram does and how the boxes are arranged: routers, switches, firewalls, IPS, APs, controllers, endpoints, servers and PoE, built into campus, data center, WAN, SOHO and cloud designs.
objectives: Name the job and layer of each component on the blueprint
Explain how PoE powers devices and check a switch power budget
Compare two-tier, three-tier and spine-leaf designs and count their links
Recognize leased line, Metro Ethernet, MPLS, internet VPN and SOHO designs
Choose between on-premises and cloud for a described situation

sections.title: Follow one click through the network
sections.key: Every device on a request's path does one job at one layer: switches forward by MAC address, routers by IP address, firewalls by session and application.
sections.body:
A laptop on the third floor of an office opens a web app in a public cloud. In half a second, that request touches almost every device on the CCNA blueprint.

[[visual]]

The laptop is an **endpoint**. The **access switch** powers the AP with **PoE**. The **distribution switch** is a **Layer 3 switch** and the users' default gateway, so it makes the first decision by IP address. A **wireless LAN controller (WLC)** manages the APs off to the side.

Exam questions here come down to two checks: what job is described, and which layer it lives at.

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: From a laptop to a cloud server
What each box decides with
rows: Bridges Wi-Fi clients onto the wired LAN
Forwards frames inside a LAN by MAC address
Switches by MAC in a VLAN, routes by IP between VLANs
Forwards packets between networks by IP address
Enforces security policy on sessions and applications
Provides services such as DNS, web or file storage

sections.tip: Underline the verb in a question: forwards frames, routes packets, filters sessions, powers devices, manages APs. The verb gives you the device.
sections.pitfall: Calling every box a router. Ask what it decides with: MAC addresses (switch, AP), IP addresses (router, Layer 3 switch), sessions and applications (firewall, IPS).

activity.title: Watch the request travel
activity.prompt: Step through the journey one hop at a time. At every device, say out loud which header it reads (MAC or IP) before you advance. Notice that the switch never changes the IP header and the router builds a brand new Ethernet frame.

check.question: The laptop in the diagram sends a packet to the cloud server. Which device makes the first forwarding decision based on the destination IP address?
choices: The access point
The access switch
The Layer 3 distribution switch acting as default gateway
The wireless LAN controller
check.explanation: The AP and the access switch move frames using Layer 2 information only. The first device that looks at the destination IP address and picks a route is the default gateway, here the Layer 3 distribution switch. The WLC manages APs; it is not in the forwarding path for this wired uplink.

sections.title: Routers, Layer 2 switches and Layer 3 switches
sections.key: Switches connect devices inside a network, routers connect networks, and a Layer 3 switch does both, routing between VLANs in hardware with SVIs.
sections.body:
Forty PCs on one floor plug into a **Layer 2 switch** and can talk at once. It forwards by destination MAC, learns locations from source MACs, floods frames it cannot place, and stays inside one VLAN. It never looks at IP addresses.

A second site across town is a different subnet, so it needs a **router**. Routers forward by IP address and never forward broadcasts: each router interface ends a broadcast domain. They sit at the WAN edge because they offer WAN interfaces and edge services such as NAT and VPNs.

A **Layer 3 switch** (multilayer switch) routes between VLANs through **switched virtual interfaces (SVIs)** at full speed, which is why distribution and core switches are usually Layer 3. Enable routing with `ip routing`:

[[code]]

[[visual]]

visual.title: Three forwarding devices
rows: MAC in a VLAN, IP between VLANs
Drops it unless a default route exists

sections.code:
D1(config)# ip routing
D1(config)# interface vlan 10
D1(config-if)# ip address 10.1.10.1 255.255.255.0
D1(config-if)# interface vlan 20
D1(config-if)# ip address 10.1.20.1 255.255.255.0
sections.pitfall: Saying a switch routes frames. A Layer 2 switch only switches inside a VLAN. Traffic between VLANs always needs a Layer 3 device: a router or a Layer 3 switch.

activity.title: Put each device on its layer
activity.prompt: Drag the devices first (hub, switch, router, firewall), then the protocols and PDUs. Pay attention to where you put the Layer 3 switch idea: it lives on two layers at once because it switches and routes.

check.question: Users in VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 on the same campus need fast routing between the two VLANs. Which device is the usual choice?
choices: A Layer 2 access switch with both VLANs configured
A Layer 3 switch with an SVI in each VLAN
A hub connecting both VLANs
An access point with two SSIDs
check.explanation: A Layer 3 switch routes between VLANs in hardware using one SVI per VLAN as each VLAN's default gateway. A Layer 2 switch can carry both VLANs but cannot route between them, and an AP with two SSIDs only maps each SSID to a VLAN.

sections.title: Firewalls, next-generation firewalls and IPS
sections.key: A stateful firewall remembers sessions so replies get back in; an NGFW adds application, URL and malware checks; an IPS drops attacks inline while an IDS only alerts.
sections.body:
A router forwards anything it has a route for. At the internet edge you want users' traffic to go out and come back, and strangers' traffic to stay out. That is a **firewall's** job.

A **stateful firewall** filters on addresses and ports and remembers sessions: when a user opens a website, the server's replies are let back in although no rule permits inbound web traffic. Interfaces sit in **zones**, with public servers in a **DMZ**.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

A **next-generation firewall (NGFW)**, such as Cisco Secure Firewall (Firepower), adds deeper checks:

[[visual 3]]

[[visual 4]]

visual.title: Zone rules
rows: Only HTTPS to the web server
Denied unless it is a reply to an inside session
visual.caption: If the DMZ server is compromised, the firewall still guards the inside zone.

visual.title: What an NGFW adds
rows: Identifies the real app, even one hiding on port 443, and applies rules per app
Allows or blocks sites by category and reputation
Intrusion prevention in the same box
Checks files against known and suspected malware

items.title: IPS
points: Matches traffic against **signatures** of known attacks

items.title: NGIPS
points: Knows the hosts and operating systems on the network
Rates how relevant an attack is
Blocks known bad addresses by reputation

sections.pitfall: Thinking a firewall is just a router with an ACL. An ACL checks each packet alone, with no memory. A stateful firewall remembers sessions, which lets replies in while blocking unsolicited traffic.

check.question: Which statement best separates an IPS from an IDS?
choices: An IPS only alerts; an IDS can drop traffic
An IPS works at Layer 2 only; an IDS works at Layer 7 only
An IPS filters by port numbers; an IDS filters by MAC address
An IPS sits inline and can drop matching traffic; an IDS watches a copy and alerts
check.explanation: Prevention requires being in the path. An IPS is inline, so it can drop a malicious packet before it arrives. An IDS receives a copy of the traffic (for example from a SPAN port), so it can detect and alert but not block.

sections.title: Access points and controllers
sections.key: An AP bridges 802.11 clients onto a wired VLAN; lightweight APs hand their management to a WLC over CAPWAP, while autonomous APs are configured one by one.
sections.body:
A hotel needs Wi-Fi in 300 rooms: dozens of **access points (APs)**. An AP converts 802.11 frames from wireless clients into 802.3 Ethernet frames and bridges them onto the VLAN mapped to each network name (**SSID**).

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

The blueprint word **controllers** also covers **SDN controllers** such as Cisco Catalyst Center (formerly DNA Center). Either way, a controller is one central brain that configures and monitors many devices, so you stop logging in to each one.

[[visual 3]]

items.title: Autonomous AP
points: Holds its own SSIDs, security and channel
Fine for a home, painful for 60 APs

items.title: Lightweight AP
points: The WLC pushes config, picks channels and power, authenticates clients and smooths roaming

items.title: Cloud-managed AP
points: Controller lives in a cloud dashboard

visual.title: Two kinds of controller
rows: Appliance (Catalyst 9800), VM, cloud, or embedded in a switch or AP
Catalyst Center: **southbound** to devices (SSH, NETCONF, RESTCONF), **northbound** REST APIs for automation

sections.tip: Autonomous AP: configured by itself. Lightweight AP: needs a WLC. If a question mentions CAPWAP, a controller is involved.
sections.pitfall: Treating an AP as a router. An AP bridges wireless clients onto a VLAN. The clients' default gateway is still a router or Layer 3 switch on the wired side.

check.question: A company has 120 lightweight APs. Which device pushes their configuration and coordinates roaming?
choices: The core router
The DHCP server
The access switch each AP is plugged into
A wireless LAN controller
check.explanation: Lightweight APs depend on a WLC. They form CAPWAP tunnels to it, and the WLC supplies configuration, RF management and roaming coordination. The access switch only gives the AP a port, a VLAN and PoE.

sections.title: Endpoints, servers and Power over Ethernet
sections.key: PoE sends power down the data cable from the switch (PSE) to an AP, phone or camera (PD), but only after detecting and classifying the device.
sections.body:
**Endpoints** are what people and things use: laptops, phones, printers, IP phones, security cameras, IoT sensors. **Servers** provide services to them (web, email, files, DNS, DHCP), often as virtual machines.

Ceiling APs and cameras have no power outlets nearby. **Power over Ethernet (PoE)** sends DC power down the UTP data cable. The switch is the **power sourcing equipment (PSE)**, the device the **powered device (PD)**. A stuck AP can be power-cycled by bouncing its port.

[[visual]]

A laptop on a PoE port simply gets no power.

[[visual 2]]

On Catalyst switches PoE is on by default (`power inline auto`). `power inline never` disables it on a port. Every switch has a total **power budget**, shown by `show power inline`:

[[code]]

visual.title: How a switch powers a device

steps.label: Detect
steps.detail: A low-voltage test looks for a powered device signature

steps.label: Classify
steps.detail: Learn how much power the device needs

steps.label: Power
steps.detail: Apply power for that class so the device boots

steps.label: Monitor
steps.detail: Keep watching; CDP or LLDP can request a different amount

visual.title: PoE standards (watts at the switch port)
visual.caption: PoE and PoE+ use two wire pairs; UPoE and UPoE+ use all four. Some Cisco material rounds UPoE+ to 100 W.

sections.code:
SW1# show power inline
Module  Available  Used    Remaining
        (Watts)    (Watts) (Watts)
1       370.0      37.0    333.0
Interface Admin Oper Power Device
Gi1/0/1   auto  on   7.0   IP Phone 8845
Gi1/0/2   auto  on   30.0  AIR-AP2802I-B-K9
Gi1/0/3   auto  off  0.0   n/a
sections.pitfall: Assuming every port can power a full-load device at once. A 48-port PoE+ switch with a 370 W budget gives 30 W to only 12 ports. Check the remaining watts before adding APs.

check.question: In a PoE link between a switch and an IP phone, which device is the PSE?
choices: The IP phone
The switch
The power outlet behind the switch
The WLC
check.explanation: The power sourcing equipment is the device that supplies power over the cable, normally the switch. The phone that receives the power is the powered device (PD).

sections.title: Campus designs: two-tier, three-tier and topology words
sections.key: Campus LANs are built in tiers: access for endpoints, distribution to aggregate and route, core as a fast backbone; two-tier, or collapsed core, folds the core into distribution.
sections.body:
A company has 1,000 users on several floors. Linking every access switch to every other would take hundreds of cables, so campus LANs are built in tiers.

[[visual]]

A **two-tier** design, also called a **collapsed core**, is the most common. Each access switch has one uplink to each of two distribution switches, and access switches never connect to each other.

[[visual 2]]

A **three-tier** design adds a core once there are enough distribution blocks (say one per building) that linking each pair would waste costly fiber.

[[visual 3]]

visual.title: Campus layers
rows: Where endpoints and APs connect; PoE, port security and VLANs live here
Aggregates access switches, routes between VLANs, applies policy; usually Layer 3 switches
High-speed backbone between distribution blocks; does nothing fancy so it stays fast

visual.title: Topology words
rows: One central device with links radiating out, like an access switch and its endpoints
Every node links to every other: N(N - 1) / 2 links, so 6 switches need 15
Some pairs linked, not all, like access-to-distribution uplinks
A mix: nearly every real design

sections.pitfall: Plugging servers or user PCs into core switches. Endpoints connect at the access layer (or to leaves in a data center). Keeping the core free of endpoints keeps it simple and fast.

check.question: What is another name for a two-tier campus design?
choices: Spine-leaf
Full mesh
Collapsed core
Hub and spoke
check.explanation: A two-tier design merges the core and distribution roles into the distribution switches, so it is called a collapsed core. Spine-leaf is a data center design and hub and spoke is a WAN topology.

sections.title: Data center designs: spine-leaf
sections.key: In spine-leaf, every leaf links to every spine, spines and leaves never link among themselves, and endpoints attach only to leaves, so servers are always leaf, spine, leaf apart.
sections.body:
In a campus most traffic runs **north-south**, users out to servers and the internet. In a **data center** most runs **east-west**, server to server: a web VM calls an app VM that calls a database VM.

The **spine-leaf** design (a Clos fabric) is built for that, with strict rules:

- Every **leaf** connects to every **spine**.
- No spine-to-spine and no leaf-to-leaf links.
- Endpoints (servers, firewalls, routers to the outside) connect only to leaves. One facing the outside is a **border leaf**.

[[visual]]

Traffic between leaves always crosses exactly three switches, and the routed spine links are all used at once (equal-cost multipath). More ports: add a leaf. More bandwidth: add a spine. Cisco ACI requires this topology.

[[visual 2]]

steps.label: Each leaf links to every spine
Multiply by the number of leaves

sections.deeper: Older data centers copied the campus design: **top-of-rack (ToR)** switches in each rack uplinked to **end-of-row (EoR)** or aggregation switches, with spanning tree blocking many of the redundant links. That suited north-south traffic but gave server-to-server flows uneven paths and wasted bandwidth, which is what spine-leaf fixes.
sections.tip: Growing the fabric is predictable: a new leaf needs one link to each spine, and a new spine needs one link to each leaf.
sections.pitfall: Connecting a server or firewall to a spine because it is closer to everything. Only leaves attach endpoints; spines only connect leaves, which keeps every path leaf, spine, leaf.

check.question: Which link breaks the rules of a spine-leaf design?
choices: A link directly between two spine switches
A link from a leaf to every spine
A server connected to a leaf switch
A firewall connected to a border leaf
check.explanation: In spine-leaf, spines never connect to each other and leaves never connect to each other. Every leaf links to every spine, and all endpoints, including firewalls and routers, attach to leaves.

sections.title: WAN architectures
sections.key: WAN services differ in what they carry and their topology: leased lines and E-Line are point-to-point, E-LAN full mesh, E-Tree hub and spoke, MPLS routed between CE routers.
sections.body:
A **WAN** connects distant sites over a service provider's network.

[[visual]]

In an **MPLS VPN**, each site's **customer edge (CE)** router connects to the provider's **provider edge (PE)** router and runs its routing protocol (OSPF, for example) with the PE, not with the other CEs. The provider routes the traffic privately and can apply QoS.

[[visual 2]]

An **internet VPN** builds encrypted IPsec tunnels over ordinary internet access: cheap and everywhere, but no guarantees. Remote users use **remote-access VPNs**.

[[visual 3]]

[[visual 4]]

visual.title: WAN services
rows: Bits on a private circuit (historically serial)
Hub and spoke, root to leaves
Ethernet frames, leaves reach only the root
IP packets, routed by the provider
visual.caption: E-Line, E-LAN and E-Tree are **Metro Ethernet** (MetroE) services defined by the MEF. Sites connect with Ethernet access links, often fiber such as 1000BASE-LX.

visual.title: Internet access for a site
rows: The telephone line, to a DSLAM at the provider

visual.title: Internet link redundancy
rows: Two links to the same ISP
Links to two or more ISPs
Two links to each of two ISPs
visual.caption: WANs use LAN topology words too: point-to-point, **hub and spoke** (branches reach each other through headquarters), full and partial mesh.

sections.tip: Metro Ethernet carries frames, so all sites on an E-LAN can share one subnet; an MPLS VPN carries IP packets routed by the provider.
sections.pitfall: Expecting an internet VPN to give MPLS-style guarantees. Encryption makes the internet private enough, but nobody guarantees bandwidth, delay or QoS across it.

check.question: A company wants a WAN service where the provider routes packets privately between all of its sites, each site connecting through a customer edge router. Which service fits?
choices: Metro Ethernet E-Line
MPLS VPN
A single leased line
Cable internet with no VPN
check.explanation: In an MPLS VPN, CE routers connect to the provider edge routers and the provider routes between all sites privately. An E-Line and a leased line join only two sites, and plain internet access is not private.

sections.title: SOHO networks
sections.key: A SOHO wireless router is a router, switch, autonomous AP and firewall in one box, plus DHCP and NAT, behind a single ISP link.
sections.body:
A dentist's office with six staff, or someone working from home, needs no access layer or WLC. A **small office/home office (SOHO)** network folds the whole campus into one consumer **wireless router**, plus the ISP's modem or fiber terminal.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

The WAN side uses whatever the ISP provides: cable, DSL, fiber or 4G/5G. Some ISPs ship modem and router in one box.

SOHO buys simplicity, not redundancy: one link (single-homed), one box, one point of failure. Branch offices of larger companies get business routers and a second link.

visual.title: Inside the wireless router
rows: A few LAN ports for wired devices
Its own SSID and security; no WLC, no CAPWAP
Routes between the LAN and the single WAN interface
Lets inside clients connect out, blocks unsolicited inbound connections
Hands out 192.168.1.0/24 addresses, with gateway (and DNS proxy) 192.168.1.1
Lets every device share the one public address on the WAN side

sections.pitfall: Expecting a SOHO AP to join a WLC. The AP inside a consumer wireless router is autonomous: configured on the box itself, with no CAPWAP tunnel.

check.question: Which four functions does a typical SOHO wireless router combine in one device?
choices: Router, Ethernet switch, autonomous AP and firewall
Spine switch, leaf switch, WLC and IPS
Core switch, distribution switch, access switch and router
PE router, CE router, MPLS switch and modem
check.explanation: A consumer wireless router acts as a router, a small switch, an autonomous access point and a basic firewall, usually with DHCP and NAT added. The other options describe enterprise or provider roles.

sections.title: On-premises versus cloud
sections.key: On-premises means you own and run the hardware; cloud rents it with self-service and elasticity, as IaaS, PaaS or SaaS, in a public, private or hybrid cloud.
sections.body:
A startup needs ten servers next week. It can buy and rack them, or rent them from a cloud provider and have them running in minutes.

[[visual]]

NIST defines **cloud computing** by five characteristics:

[[visual 2]]

[[visual 3]]

A **public cloud** runs in the provider's data centers, shared by many customers. A **private cloud** gives your own data center the same self-service, pooled, elastic behavior. **Hybrid** mixes both.

Reaching a public cloud is a WAN choice:

[[visual 4]]

items.title: On-premises
points: Full control of hardware and where data lives
You handle power, cooling, spares and growth

items.title: Cloud
points: Pay monthly for what you use (operating expense)
Scales up and down on demand

visual.title: The five NIST characteristics
rows: You create resources through a portal or API, with no ticket to IT
Reachable over the network from many kinds of devices
One big pool of hardware shared among customers
Scale up and down quickly, so it looks unlimited

visual.title: Service models
rows: A platform that runs your code
Only your code; the provider runs OS and runtime
A finished app, such as web email
Nothing but your use of it

visual.title: Connecting to a public cloud
rows: A new circuit for each cloud provider
One private link reaching several cloud providers
Costs more than plain internet access
visual.caption: An intercloud exchange makes it easy to move workloads between providers without new circuits.

sections.pitfall: Calling any company-owned data center a private cloud. Without self-service, pooling and elasticity it is just an on-premises virtualized data center.

check.question: A developer creates three virtual servers through a web portal in five minutes without contacting IT. Which cloud characteristic does this show?
choices: Measured service
Resource pooling
On-demand self-service
Broad network access
check.explanation: Creating resources yourself, without a human in the provider's IT team doing it for you, is on-demand self-service. Measured service is about metering and billing what you use.

keyTerms.definition: A switch that also routes between VLANs in hardware using SVIs; common at the distribution and core layers.
A stateful firewall that adds application visibility and control, URL filtering, integrated IPS and malware protection.
Intrusion prevention system: sits inline, matches traffic against attack signatures and drops matches. An IDS only alerts.
Central device that configures and manages lightweight APs over CAPWAP tunnels.
Power over Ethernet: DC power sent over UTP from a PSE (usually a switch) to a powered device such as an AP, phone or camera.
A two-tier campus design where the distribution switches also perform the core role.
Data center design where every leaf connects to every spine, spines never interconnect and endpoints attach only to leaves.
WAN topology where branch sites connect only to a central site, which relays branch-to-branch traffic.
Small office/home office network, usually one consumer router that combines routing, switching, an AP and a firewall.
Cloud service models: rent VMs, rent a platform for your code, or use a finished application.
Power sourcing equipment (the PoE switch) and the powered device (AP, phone, camera) it supplies.
Server-to-server traffic inside a data center, the pattern spine-leaf is built for.
Provider WAN service that carries Ethernet frames between sites: E-Line, E-LAN or E-Tree.
Provider service that privately routes a customer's IP packets between CE routers across its MPLS network.
Customer edge router at the site and provider edge router at the edge of the provider network.
A site with two links to the same ISP; multihomed means links to two or more ISPs.

summary: Switches forward frames by MAC, routers forward packets by IP, Layer 3 switches do both.
Stateful firewalls let replies in; NGFWs add AVC, URL filtering, IPS and malware checks; an IPS drops, an IDS alerts.
Lightweight APs need a WLC over CAPWAP; PoE detects and classifies a device before powering it.
Campus: access, distribution, core (two-tier is collapsed core). Data center: spine-leaf.
WAN: leased line and E-Line point-to-point, E-LAN full mesh, E-Tree hub and spoke, MPLS routes between CEs.
SOHO is one box; cloud is self-service and elastic: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS; public, private, hybrid.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a new IT hire what happens to a web request as it leaves a laptop on Wi-Fi and reaches a cloud server, naming each device it passes and what that device decides.

questions.question: Match each network component to its main job.

pairs.right: Forwards packets between networks by IP address
Forwards frames inside a LAN by MAC address
Enforces security policy with application awareness
Centrally manages lightweight access points
Bridges Wi-Fi clients onto the wired LAN
Provides services such as DNS or file storage to clients

questions.explanation: Each component does one main job. Matching on the verb works: routers route packets, switches switch frames, firewalls enforce policy, WLCs manage APs, APs bridge radio to wire, servers serve.

questions.question: A technician says "this device reads the destination IP address, but it does not care about the Ethernet MAC address of the next hop until it has picked a route". Which device is being described?
choices: A Layer 2 access switch
A hub
A router
An access point
questions.explanation: A router makes its decision on the destination IP address, then builds a new Ethernet frame for the chosen next hop. A Layer 2 switch and an AP decide using MAC addresses, and a hub makes no decision at all.

questions.question: Which device stops Ethernet broadcasts from spreading from one LAN into another by default?
choices: A router
A Layer 2 switch
A hub
A PoE injector
questions.explanation: Routers do not forward broadcasts, so each router interface is the boundary of a broadcast domain. A Layer 2 switch floods broadcasts out every port in the VLAN, and a hub repeats everything everywhere.

questions.question: Which two statements describe a Layer 2 switch? (Choose two.)
choices: It learns MAC addresses from the source address of incoming frames
It forwards frames based on the destination IP address
It floods frames whose destination MAC address it has not learned
It separates each port into its own broadcast domain
It uses a routing table to pick the next hop
questions.explanation: A Layer 2 switch learns from source MAC addresses and floods unknown unicast frames within the VLAN. It does not read IP addresses or keep a routing table, and all ports in one VLAN share one broadcast domain.

questions.question: A multilayer switch has SVIs for VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 with IP addresses, but hosts in the two VLANs still cannot reach each other through it. Which global configuration command turns on IPv4 routing?
questions.explanation: Many Layer 3 switches ship with IPv4 routing disabled. Until you enter ip routing in global configuration mode, the switch treats its SVIs like management interfaces and does not route between them.

questions.question: A company is replacing its branch WAN edge. An engineer suggests using a Layer 3 switch instead of a router. Which is the strongest reason to keep a router at the WAN edge?
choices: Layer 3 switches cannot run routing protocols such as OSPF
Layer 3 switches cannot be given IP addresses on their interfaces
Routers switch frames inside a VLAN faster than Layer 3 switches
Routers support a wider range of WAN interfaces and edge services such as VPN termination and NAT
questions.explanation: Layer 3 switches route very fast between VLANs and can run OSPF, but routers are built for the edge: varied WAN interfaces, VPNs, NAT and other services. Switches, not routers, are the faster choice for switching inside a VLAN.

questions.question: In a typical enterprise campus, where are Layer 3 switches most often deployed?
choices: At the access layer, connecting user PCs only
At the distribution and core layers
Only inside SOHO wireless routers
Between the ISP modem and the internet
questions.explanation: Distribution and core switches carry traffic between many VLANs and buildings, so they usually route in hardware as Layer 3 switches. Access switches are often Layer 2, and the ISP connection is a router's job.

questions.question: Which device sits inline in the traffic path and can drop packets that match a known attack signature?
choices: An IPS
An IDS
A WLC
A Layer 2 switch
questions.explanation: An IPS is inline, so it can block matching traffic as it passes. An IDS analyzes a copy of the traffic and can only raise alerts.

questions.question: A user inside the network opens a website. The firewall has no rule allowing inbound web traffic, yet the web server's replies reach the user. Why?
choices: The firewall forwards all TCP traffic in both directions by default
The web server uses UDP, which firewalls never filter
The firewall tracks the session the user started and permits its return traffic
The firewall routes replies through the DMZ, which has no rules
questions.explanation: Stateful firewalls record sessions that start from trusted zones and automatically allow the matching return traffic. Unsolicited inbound connections are still denied.

questions.question: Which three features distinguish a next-generation firewall from a traditional stateful firewall? (Choose three.)
choices: Application visibility and control
Filtering by source and destination port numbers
An integrated intrusion prevention engine
Stateful tracking of TCP sessions
URL filtering by category and reputation
Network address translation
questions.explanation: NGFWs add application awareness, integrated NGIPS and URL filtering (plus malware protection). Port filtering, session state and NAT are features that traditional stateful firewalls already have.

questions.question: A company must let internet users reach its public web server while protecting internal hosts if that server is ever compromised. Where should the web server go?
choices: On the inside zone, next to the user PCs
In a DMZ zone on the firewall
On the outside of the firewall with no protection
On the same VLAN as the WLC
questions.explanation: A DMZ is a separate firewall zone for public-facing servers. Outside users may reach the server, but the server cannot freely start connections into the inside zone, which limits the damage if it is hacked.

questions.question: Which device configures lightweight access points and coordinates client roaming between them?
choices: A next-generation firewall
A DHCP server
A Layer 2 access switch
A wireless LAN controller
questions.explanation: Lightweight APs depend on a WLC for configuration, RF management and roaming. The switch only provides the AP's port, VLAN and PoE.

questions.question: Which statement about lightweight access points is true?
choices: Each one is configured separately through its own CLI or web page
They route packets between VLANs for their wireless clients
They cannot receive power through PoE
They build CAPWAP tunnels to a WLC that manages them
questions.explanation: Lightweight APs use CAPWAP to reach a WLC, which manages them centrally. Configuring each AP separately describes autonomous APs. APs bridge clients onto VLANs rather than routing, and they are usually PoE powered.

questions.question: An autonomous AP receives an 802.11 frame from a laptop addressed to a file server on the wired LAN. What does the AP do with it?
choices: Routes it using the destination IP address
Converts it to an 802.3 Ethernet frame and bridges it onto the mapped VLAN
Drops it, because wireless clients may only reach other wireless clients
Encrypts it with CAPWAP and sends it to the internet
questions.explanation: An AP is a translational bridge: it turns the 802.11 frame into an Ethernet frame and forwards it onto the wired VLAN mapped to that SSID. It does not route. An autonomous AP has no WLC, so there is no CAPWAP tunnel.

questions.question: Which of these is an endpoint?
choices: A distribution switch
A wireless LAN controller
An IP security camera
A core router
questions.explanation: Endpoints are devices at the edge that people or things use, such as PCs, phones, printers and cameras. Switches, routers and controllers are infrastructure.

questions.question: Put the steps a PoE switch takes, from the moment a device is plugged in, in order.
items: Send a low-voltage test to detect a powered device signature
Classify the device to learn how much power it needs
Apply power according to that class so the device can boot
Keep monitoring and adjust power if CDP or LLDP requests a change
questions.explanation: PoE never applies full power blindly. It detects a PD first, classifies it, powers it, then keeps watching, which is why plugging a normal laptop into a PoE port is safe.

questions.question: How many watts per port can an IEEE 802.3at (PoE+) switch port supply?
questions.explanation: PoE+ (802.3at) supplies up to 30 W at the switch port over two pairs. Original PoE (802.3af) gives about 15 W, and UPoE (802.3bt) goes to 60 W and beyond over four pairs.

questions.question: The engineer wants to add new APs that each need a full 30 W class 4 allocation, connected to SW1 shown in the exhibit. How many more of them can SW1 power?
questions.code:
SW1# show power inline
Module   Available     Used     Remaining

1            370.0       37.0       333.0
Interface Admin  Oper       Power   Device              Class Max

questions.explanation: SW1 has 333.0 W remaining. 333 / 30 = 11.1, so 11 more class 4 APs fit (330 W) and a twelfth would exceed the budget. Gi1/0/3 is off only because nothing that needs power is connected.

questions.question: In a campus LAN, which layer do user PCs and APs connect to?
choices: Core
Distribution
Access
Spine
questions.explanation: Endpoints and APs plug into access switches. Distribution switches aggregate access switches, and the core connects distribution blocks. Spine belongs to data center spine-leaf designs.

questions.question: Match each design term to its description.

pairs.right: Where endpoints and APs connect
Aggregates access switches and routes between VLANs
High-speed backbone between distribution blocks
Every node has a link to every other node
Some pairs of nodes are linked, but not all
One central device with links radiating out to the others

questions.explanation: The tiers describe roles in a campus. Star, full mesh and partial mesh describe link patterns. A two-tier campus mixes stars (access) and a partial mesh (uplinks), so it is a hybrid.

questions.question: A WAN design connects 8 routers in a full mesh, one link between each pair. How many links are needed?
questions.explanation: A full mesh of N nodes needs N(N - 1) / 2 links: 8 x 7 / 2 = 28. This fast growth is why large designs use a partial mesh or add a core.

questions.question: A campus has grown to six buildings, each with its own pair of distribution switches. Why would the designer add a core layer?
choices: To avoid a growing mesh of costly links between every pair of distribution blocks
To give users in each building a place to plug in
To replace the need for VLANs in each building
Because two-tier designs cannot route between VLANs
questions.explanation: Connecting six distribution blocks to each other directly needs many inter-building links, usually expensive fiber. A core lets each block connect only to the core switches. Two-tier designs route between VLANs just fine.

questions.question: Which two statements about a spine-leaf design are true? (Choose two.)
choices: Every leaf switch connects to every spine switch
Spine switches connect to each other in a full mesh
Servers connect only to leaf switches
Servers connect to spine switches to reduce latency
Traffic between two leaves crosses at least two spines
questions.explanation: Leaves connect to every spine, spines never interconnect, and all endpoints attach to leaves. Leaf-to-leaf traffic crosses exactly one spine, which is what makes latency predictable.

questions.question: A spine-leaf fabric has 4 spine switches and 20 leaf switches, with one link between each leaf and each spine. How many leaf-to-spine links are there?
questions.explanation: Every leaf connects to every spine, so the count is leaves x spines = 20 x 4 = 80. No spine-to-spine or leaf-to-leaf links are added.

questions.question: In a spine-leaf fabric, a server on Leaf1 sends to a server on Leaf3. How many switches does the traffic pass through?
questions.explanation: The path is always leaf, spine, leaf: three switches. That fixed path length gives every server pair the same latency.

questions.question: Which description fits a typical SOHO network?
choices: A spine-leaf fabric with a dedicated WLC
A three-tier design with redundant core switches
An MPLS network operated by the customer
One consumer wireless router acting as router, switch, AP and firewall, connected to the ISP
questions.explanation: Small office/home office networks usually rely on a single all-in-one device plus a modem or fiber connection to the ISP. The other options describe enterprise or provider designs.

questions.question: Twelve branch offices each have one WAN link to headquarters. Branch-to-branch traffic travels through headquarters. Which WAN topology is this?
choices: Full mesh
Hub and spoke
Spine-leaf
Collapsed core
questions.explanation: A central hub with branches (spokes) that only connect to it is hub and spoke. A full mesh would give every branch a direct link to every other branch.

questions.question: A company wants private connectivity between its sites over a provider network. The provider should route the company's traffic between sites, with each site connecting through its customer edge router and no internet exposure. Which service fits?
choices: An MPLS VPN
An internet VPN over DSL
A single leased line between two sites
A SOHO wireless router at each site
questions.explanation: In an MPLS VPN, customer edge routers connect to the provider's edge routers, and the provider routes the customer's traffic privately across its MPLS network between all sites. An internet VPN crosses the public internet, and one leased line only joins two sites.

questions.question: A team rents virtual machines from a cloud provider and installs and patches the operating system themselves. Which service model is this?
choices: SaaS
PaaS
IaaS
On-premises
questions.explanation: Infrastructure as a Service gives you VMs; you manage the OS and everything above it. With PaaS the provider runs the OS and runtime, and with SaaS you only use the finished application.

questions.question: Match each cloud term to its description.

pairs.right: Rent VMs and manage the OS yourself
Deploy your code; the provider runs the OS and runtime
Use a finished application, often through a browser
Provider data centers shared by many customers
Self-service, pooled resources inside your own data center

questions.explanation: Service models describe who manages what. Deployment models describe whose data center it is and who shares it.

questions.question: Which is a typical advantage of on-premises infrastructure compared with public cloud?
choices: No hardware purchases are needed
Full control over the hardware and where data physically lives
Capacity can grow in minutes without buying anything
Usage is metered and billed monthly
questions.explanation: On-premises means you own and control the equipment and the location of your data. Avoiding hardware purchases, rapid elasticity and metered billing are cloud advantages.

questions.question: A company needs a private, QoS-capable connection to its public cloud provider and wants to be able to move workloads to a second cloud provider later without ordering new WAN circuits. Which option fits best?
choices: The public internet with no VPN
An internet VPN to the first provider
A private WAN link directly to the first provider
An intercloud exchange
questions.explanation: An intercloud exchange gives one private connection to an exchange that already connects to several cloud providers, so switching providers does not need new circuits. A direct private WAN link is private and QoS-capable but tied to one provider.

questions.question: Which kind of controller centralizes management of switches, routers and APs and offers northbound REST APIs to automation tools?
choices: A wireless LAN controller
An SDN controller such as Cisco Catalyst Center
A DHCP server
A PoE injector
questions.explanation: An SDN controller such as Cisco Catalyst Center manages many kinds of devices and exposes northbound APIs. A WLC manages wireless APs only, and the other two are not controllers.

questions.question: A camera on Gi1/0/9 must never receive PoE, even if it requests it. Which interface subcommand disables PoE on that port?
questions.explanation: power inline never turns PoE off on the port. power inline auto, the default, detects and powers PDs automatically.

questions.question: A new AP on Gi1/0/6 never boots, while an identical AP on Gi1/0/5 works. Based on the exhibit, what is the cause?
questions.code:
SW1# show power inline
Module   Available     Used     Remaining
          (Watts)     (Watts)    (Watts)
------   ---------   --------   ---------
1            370.0       67.0       303.0
Interface Admin  Oper       Power   Device              Class Max
                            (Watts)
--------- ------ ---------- ------- ------------------- ----- ----
Gi1/0/5   auto   on         30.0    AIR-AP2802I-B-K9    4     30.0
Gi1/0/6   never  off        0.0     n/a                 n/a   30.0
choices: The switch has run out of power budget
Gi1/0/6 is a 15 W port that cannot power the AP
PoE is disabled on Gi1/0/6 by configuration
The AP on Gi1/0/6 is not a powered device
questions.explanation: Admin "never" means PoE has been disabled on Gi1/0/6 with power inline never, so the port will not power anything. The budget has plenty of watts left, and Gi1/0/5 shows the same AP model drawing 30 W normally. Fix it with power inline auto.

questions.question: About how many watts can an IEEE 802.3af (original PoE) switch port supply?
questions.explanation: 802.3af supplies 15.4 W at the switch port, usually rounded to 15 W, over two pairs. PoE+ (802.3at) doubles that to 30 W.

questions.question: In a data center, what does east-west traffic mean?
choices: Traffic between servers inside the data center
Traffic between users and the internet
Traffic that crosses the WAN between two data centers
Management traffic to the console port
questions.explanation: East-west traffic flows between servers inside the data center, such as a web VM calling a database VM. North-south traffic enters or leaves the data center. Spine-leaf is designed for heavy east-west traffic.

questions.question: Match each WAN service to the topology it provides.

pairs.right: Point-to-point between two sites
Full mesh, any site to any site
Hub and spoke, root to leaves
Provider routes IP packets between CE routers

questions.explanation: E-Line is a point-to-point Ethernet circuit, E-LAN lets every site reach every other site directly, E-Tree lets one root reach all leaves while leaves reach only the root, and in an MPLS VPN the provider routes IP packets between CE routers.

questions.question: A company has an MPLS VPN connecting five sites and runs OSPF at every site. With which device does the branch CE router form its OSPF neighbor relationship?
choices: The CE routers at the other four sites
Only the headquarters CE router
The provider edge (PE) router it connects to
No neighbor, because MPLS VPNs do not support routing protocols
questions.explanation: In an MPLS VPN the CE router peers with the provider edge router it connects to, and the provider carries the routes to the other sites. The CE routers do not become neighbors with each other directly.

questions.question: A branch connects to the internet with two links, both to the same ISP. Which term describes this design?
choices: Single-homed
Dual-homed
Multihomed
Dual multihomed
questions.explanation: Dual-homed means two connections to the same ISP. Single-homed is one link to one ISP, multihomed means links to two or more ISPs, and dual multihomed means two links to each of two ISPs.

questions.question: Which internet access technology delivers data over the existing telephone line, with a DSLAM at the provider end?
choices: Cable internet
DSL
Fiber Ethernet
4G/5G wireless
questions.explanation: DSL uses the copper telephone line and a DSL access multiplexer (DSLAM) in the telco office. Cable internet uses the TV coax, and 4G/5G uses cellular radio.

questions.question: A consumer wireless router serves a home office. Which four functions does it typically perform? (Choose four.)
choices: Routing between the LAN and the internet
Ethernet switching for wired devices
Wireless LAN controller for lightweight APs
Autonomous access point
Firewall blocking unsolicited inbound connections
Spine switch for a leaf fabric
questions.explanation: One SOHO box acts as a router, a small Ethernet switch, an autonomous AP and a firewall, and usually adds DHCP and NAT. It does not act as a WLC for other APs, and spine switching belongs to data centers.

questions.question: A home wireless router hands out addresses in 192.168.1.0/24 and its LAN address is 192.168.1.1. Its WAN port has the ISP-assigned address 203.0.113.77. What default gateway do the home devices receive?
choices: The ISP's router address
questions.explanation: Clients need a gateway on their own subnet, so the router gives them its LAN address, 192.168.1.1. The router then uses NAT to translate their private addresses to 203.0.113.77 on the way out.
